html:
A Roman welfare program that paid for food and support for poor children in towns across Italy. It probably began under Nerva around 98 CE, was greatly expanded by Trajan, and lasted until about 272 CE.

It worked like an endowment. The imperial treasury lent money to Italian landowners against their land at a low rate of interest. The interest was paid to the local town, which used it to give monthly allowances to children. Boys got more than girls, and children of citizens more than those born outside marriage. A large bronze tablet from Veleia, near Piacenza, lists the loans and the children supported there.

Why the emperors did it is debated. It may have been charity, a way to help Italian farming, or a way to raise more future soldiers. Trajan advertised it on coins and on his arch at Benevento.

Later emperors kept it going, and Antoninus Pius set up a fund for girls in memory of his wife. Like the older Roman grain dole, it shows the state taking on care of the poor. It faded away in the money troubles of the Crisis of the Third Century.
sum: A Roman welfare program that paid for food and support for poor children in towns across Italy. It probably began under Nerva around 98 CE, was greatly expanded by Trajan, and lasted until about 272 CE.
